blocks.text: Some operations take real time, generating a long report, processing a large file.
Waiting silently for one final response can feel broken, even when everything is working correctly.
Streaming solves this by letting a server send partial progress while the real work is still happening.
1. Streaming Is Not a Separate Message Type

blocks.alt: A progress notification precedes a final response

blocks.text: MCP has no special streaming message.
Streaming is built entirely from notifications, sent while a request is still in flight, followed eventually by the normal, final response to that request.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: This reuse keeps the protocol small, one message type, notifications, does double duty for both progress reporting and ordinary one way announcements.

blocks.text: Nothing new had to be added to the wire format for this to work.
That is the underlying reason this pattern feels so natural once you already understand notifications.
2. The Basic Pattern

blocks.alt: A tool call request produces progress updates before a final result

blocks.text: A client sends a request as usual.
Before the final response arrives, the server can send one or more progress notifications describing how far along the work has gotten.
Notice the request keeps its own id throughout, the notifications reference that same id, and the final response echoes it one last time.
This same sequence works identically whether the underlying transport is stdio or an HTTP based connection.
3. Why This Piggybacks on Notifications
Notifications already have no id and expect no reply.
That is exactly the shape a progress update needs, informational, one way, and safe to send any number of times without confusing the request-response bookkeeping already in place.

code.content:
# a notification has no id, exactly what an update needs
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/progress", "params": {"requestId": 8, "percent": 60}}

blocks.text: Inventing a fourth message type just for this would have added complexity without adding real capability.
4. Linking a Progress Update Back to Its Request

blocks.alt: A progress update links back to a request id

blocks.text: A progress notification includes a requestId field pointing back at the original request it describes.
This lets a client correctly route an incoming update to the right progress bar, even if several long-running calls are happening at once.
Without this field, a client watching two slow calls at once would have no way to tell which update belongs to which.

code.content:
# routing an incoming update to the right progress bar
progress_bars[msg["params"]["requestId"]].update(msg["params"]["percent"])

blocks.text: The same field name and matching logic apply no matter how many long running calls are active at once.
5. The Final Response Still Behaves Normally
No matter how many progress notifications arrived along the way, the request still ends with exactly one ordinary response, matched by id, containing a result or an error.
Streaming only adds visibility into the wait, it does not change how the request itself concludes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Property","Streaming call","Ordinary call"],"rows":[["Has an id","Yes","Yes"],["Gets exactly one final response","Yes","Yes"],["May emit notifications first","Yes","No"]]}

blocks.text: A client that only ever listens for the final response, ignoring every progress update, still works correctly, it simply loses the visibility streaming provides.
6. Streaming Is Optional

blocks.alt: A server supporting streaming is compared against no streaming at all

blocks.text: Not every tool needs it, and not every server implements it.
A quick lookup has nothing meaningful to report partway through, streaming is worth building specifically for operations that genuinely take noticeable time.
Checking for this capability before relying on it, the same way any other optional feature is checked, avoids assuming updates that will never actually arrive.
A tool description can simply note whether it supports progress updates, so a client knows what to expect.
Building it into every tool by default, even ones that finish instantly, adds needless complexity for no real benefit.
7. What a Client Does With Progress Updates
A host application typically uses these updates to show a progress bar or a status message to the user.
A model itself does not usually need to see every incremental update, only the host layer does, until the final result is ready.
A well designed host debounces frequent updates before repainting the screen, avoiding a progress bar that flickers unpleasantly.

blocks.text: 8. Streaming Content vs Streaming Progress

blocks.alt: Streaming content is compared against streaming progress

blocks.text: Progress notifications report how far along something is.

Some tools instead stream the actual content itself, partial text as it is generated, sent as a series of notifications before one final, complete result, the same underlying mechanism, used for a slightly different purpose.

code.content:
# streaming partial text content instead of a percentage
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/progress", "params": {"requestId": 8, "partial_text": "The quarterly revenue grew..."}}

blocks.text: Both variants reuse the exact same notification mechanism, only the shape of the params differs.
9. Handling a Server That Stops Sending Updates
A gap in progress notifications does not necessarily mean something broke.
A client should rely on the request timeout, covered in the Timeouts lesson, rather than treating a quiet stretch between updates as a failure on its own.
A long silent gap followed by the correct final result is still a success, the timeout exists specifically to catch the case where nothing ever arrives at all.
Treating silence as failure too eagerly risks cancelling work that was actually about to finish successfully.
This is one more reason a sensible timeout, not the absence of updates, should always be the real signal something has gone wrong.
10. Cancelling a Streamed Operation Midway

blocks.alt: A streamed operation gets cancelled midway and stops

blocks.text: The same cancellation notification covered in the Requests lesson works here too.
A client watching progress updates can decide, based on what it sees, to cancel a call that is taking longer than the user is willing to wait for.
Watching a report reach only ten percent after the expected total time has already passed is exactly the kind of signal that might prompt a cancellation.
The server should stop its work promptly once a cancellation arrives, rather than continuing to send updates for a call the client no longer cares about.
11. Designing Good Progress Updates
A useful progress update carries enough detail to be meaningful, a percentage, a stage name, without being so frequent that it floods the connection with noise.
A handful of well-timed updates communicate progress far better than a hundred nearly identical ones.

blocks.title: A practical guideline
blocks.content: A handful of updates spaced across the operation, not a constant stream every few milliseconds, is usually the right balance.

blocks.text: Naming a stage, like uploading or transcoding, alongside a percentage often communicates more than a bare number alone.
12. A Worked Example

blocks.alt: A client sends a tool call, receives progress, then a result

blocks.text: Trace a report generation call from start to finish, including two progress updates along the way.

code.content:
client.call_tool_async("generate_report", {}, on_progress=lambda p: print(f"{p}% done"))
# 40% done
# 80% done
# final result returned

blocks.text: The same pattern extends naturally to any operation with distinct, nameable phases a user would find genuinely reassuring to see.

blocks.title: Worth trying
blocks.content: Add a third progress update partway between the two shown here and confirm the client still routes it correctly by requestId.

blocks.text: 13. Common Mistakes When Using Streaming

items: Sending so many progress notifications that they overwhelm the connection instead of helping.
Forgetting to include the requestId, leaving a client unable to match an update to the right call.
Treating a gap in updates as an automatic failure instead of relying on a proper timeout.
Building streaming for a fast operation that never actually needed it in the first place.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is streaming a percentage that never actually reflects real progress, which erodes trust faster than no progress indicator at all.
A sixth common mistake is sending a progress value that jumps backward, which reads as a bug even when the underlying work is fine.
Testing the update sequence deliberately, not just the final result, catches these issues before real users see them.
14. Practice: Add Progress to a Slow Tool
Sketch what progress notifications a video transcoding tool might send, covering roughly three or four meaningful stages from start to finish.
Consider what would happen if the transcoding step failed partway through, and how the final error response should relate to the progress already shown.
Try also sketching the final error response your tool would send if transcoding failed at the second stage.
Key Takeaway
Streaming in MCP is built entirely from ordinary notifications sent while a request is still open, each linked back to that request by id, followed eventually by one normal final response.

This lesson builds on Notifications and Requests from earlier in this module, and connects forward to Event Handling next, which covers how a client actually listens for and reacts to these incoming updates in practice.

Keep this notification based design in mind, it is the same lightweight mechanism used for resource change alerts elsewhere in this curriculum, just applied here to reporting progress on a single request.
